moves.spoken: White plays the King's Gambit — f4, offering the pawn to rip open the center at the cost of weakening his own kingside.
We take the pawn, then play d5. The point is simple: f4 weakened White's kingside, and the principle is to open the center to exploit that weakness.
teaches: ...d5 to open the center against f4

moves.spoken: We don't recapture d5 with the queen — that would allow a knight to c3 kicking it and boosting White's development. The knight to f6 takes it instead, keeping the queen safe and even lending support to our f4-pawn.
teaches: recapture with the knight, keep the queen safe

moves.spoken: The knight recaptures on d5, comfortably ahead.
The bishop to c4 can't touch the knight.
The bishop to e7 looks passive, but it's perfectly fine — we're up a pawn, so there's no need to develop aggressively.
teaches: solid development is enough when ahead

moves.spoken: Here's the key theme — transforming the advantage. We're happy to give the pawn back for lasting positional pluses, and that's exactly why the King's Gambit isn't the terror it was once thought to be: Black can hand the pawn back and get compensation.
teaches: give the pawn back for positional gains

moves.spoken: The bishop to e6 blunts the annoying bishop on c4 — killing its x-ray on our knight and its pressure on f7.
The far-sighted move is the knight to c6.

After the trade we recapture with the b-pawn. The doubled c-pawns look ugly but are a bargaining chip — they roll forward one after the other to contest the center, and they can be undoubled later with c5 and a queen recapture on d4.
teaches: doubled pawns as a dynamic bargaining chip
